Validation report

Source: vignettes/validation.Rmd
validation.Rmd

This report states what was checked, against what, and how close the numbers are. Checks are of three kinds:

  • Exact agreement with an independent implementation (vars, BVAR, lpirfs, lm + sandwich, closed-form or quadrature results). These run live in this document (section 2), so the numbers below are recomputed every time the vignette is built.
  • Statistical agreement (Monte Carlo error, Geweke joint-distribution tests, simulation-based calibration, coverage simulations). These take minutes, so section 3 quotes the output of the scripts in validation/, with the exact command that reproduces each block.
  • Known failures and limitations found by those checks (section 5). They are listed because a validation report that only shows passes is not informative.

Numbers quoted in section 3 and 4 were produced on an Apple M4 Pro, R 4.6.1, macOS 26.6, OpenBLAS, with the version of the code in this repository. They are single runs with the seeds in the scripts; Monte Carlo errors are noted where they matter.

1. How to run everything

From the package root:

# unit tests (846 expectations; about 15 s)
Rscript validation/run-all.R                    # same as testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")

# heavier validation scripts (not run by run-all.R)
Rscript validation/bayes.R                      # sections s1-s8 and s2d, about 3 min
Rscript validation/bayes.R s5 s7                # a subset of sections
Rscript validation/ident-extra.R                # about 5 s
Rscript validation/proxy-bayes-full.R           # reps T (default 50, 300), about 5 s
Rscript validation/proxy-coverage.R 200 199 200 # reps nboot T, about 5 s
Rscript validation/lp-extra.R                   # about 10 s
Rscript validation/tvp.R                        # about 4 min

validation/run-all.R runs only tests/testthat. The scripts in validation/ print [PASS]/[FAIL] lines (bayes.R) or raw numbers for inspection (the others); they are not wired into R CMD check. The reference packages are listed under Suggests; tests that need one skip when it is missing (svars is listed but not installed on the machine used here, and no check in this report uses it).

At the time of writing the test suite gives 846 expectations / 0 failures / 5 skips (about 15 s), over ten files. The skips are the comparisons against vars, lpirfs and psvar, which did not load on the machine used for this update (see section 6):

file covers
test-var.R OLS, logLik, IC, stability, Cholesky IRF/FEVD, Blanchard-Quah, forecasts vs vars; bootstrap variants; edge cases and error messages
test-bayes.R triangular sampler vs exact posterior, SV (Geweke), SSVS/horseshoe, fixed-hyperparameter NIW moments, Haar rotations, MC covariance, mcmc_diagnostics
test-bvar-conj.R hierarchical NIW log posterior vs BVAR; sampler sanity; irf/fevd/hd/forecast on bvarm
test-psvar.R proxy-SVAR vs hand computation, Mertens-Ravn B1, robust (MOSW) sets, block bootstrap, Bayesian proxy, LP-IV consistency
test-psvar-bayes-full.R varm_proxy_arw() and varm_proxy_gkr()
test-ident-extra.R id_proxy, proxy_draws, zero+sign, id_restrictions, id_hetero
test-lp.R LP coefficients and HAC/HC errors vs lm + sandwich, LP-IV vs manual 2SLS
test-lp-extra.R lp_joint, lp_supt, lp_state (vs lm+NW and lpirfs), lp_smooth, lp_panel, lp_forecast, compare_lp_var
test-tvp.R dimensions, constant limit vs OLS, methods, variants, prior calibration
test-methods.R print/summary/accessor methods, plotting

2. Live checks: agreement with reference implementations

2.1 Reduced-form VAR against vars 

if (have("vars")) {
  f <- varm(Y, p = 2)
  v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 2, type = "const")
  Bv <- sapply(v$varresult, coef)
  vs <- vars::VARselect(Y, lag.max = 6, type = "const")
  mine <- var_select(Y, 6)
  ir <- vars::irf(v, n.ahead = 12, ortho = TRUE, boot = FALSE)$irf
  fe <- vars::fevd(v, n.ahead = 13)
  m_ir <- irf(f, horizon = 12, ci = "none")$estimate
  m_fe <- fevd(f, horizon = 12, ci = "none")$estimate
  d_ir <- d_fe <- 0
  for (s in colnames(Y)) for (r in colnames(Y)) {
    d_ir <- max(d_ir, abs(unname(m_ir[r, s, ]) - ir[[s]][, r]))
    d_fe <- max(d_fe, abs(unname(m_fe[r, s, ]) - fe[[r]][, s]))
  }
  fc <- predict(v, n.ahead = 8, ci = 0.95)$fcst
  mf <- forecast(f, h = 8, ci = "none")$mean
  d_fc <- max(sapply(colnames(Y), function(k) max(abs(unname(mf[, k]) - fc[[k]][, "fcst"]))))
  res_vars <- tibble::tibble(
    quantity = c("coefficients B", "residual covariance", "log-likelihood", "information criteria (AIC, HQ, SC)",
                 "root moduli (companion)", "Cholesky IRF, h = 0..12", "FEVD, h = 0..12", "point forecast, h = 1..8"),
    max_abs_diff = c(max(abs(unname(f$B) - unname(Bv))),
                     max(abs(unname(f$Sigma) - unname(summary(v)$covres))),
                     abs(as.numeric(logLik(f)) - as.numeric(logLik(v))),
                     max(abs(unname(mine$criteria[, 1:3]) - unname(t(vs$criteria)[, 1:3]))),
                     max(abs(sort(stability(f), decreasing = TRUE) - sort(Mod(vars::roots(v)), decreasing = TRUE))),
                     d_ir, d_fe, d_fc))
  res_vars$max_abs_diff <- sci(res_vars$max_abs_diff)
  print(res_vars, n = Inf)
  cat("lag order chosen (AIC, HQ, SC, FPE): varm", mine$selection, "| vars", vs$selection, "\n")
}
#> # A tibble: 8 × 2
#>   quantity                           max_abs_diff
#>   <chr>                              <chr>       
#> 1 coefficients B                     3.9e-13     
#> 2 residual covariance                2.2e-16     
#> 3 log-likelihood                     0.0e+00     
#> 4 information criteria (AIC, HQ, SC) 2.7e-15     
#> 5 root moduli (companion)            3.8e-13     
#> 6 Cholesky IRF, h = 0..12            6.1e-13     
#> 7 FEVD, h = 0..12                    5.8e-13     
#> 8 point forecast, h = 1..8           7.1e-12     
#> lag order chosen (AIC, HQ, SC, FPE): varm 6 2 2 6 | vars 6 2 2 6

The unit tests assert agreement to 1e-9; the observed differences above are rounding-level. Lag selection is identical (the information criteria differ by rounding only).

2.2 Blanchard-Quah impact matrix against vars::BQ 

if (have("vars")) {
  bq <- vars::BQ(vars::VAR(Y[, 1:2], p = 2))
  P <- irf(varm(Y[, 1:2], p = 2), id = id_longrun(), horizon = 0, ci = "none")$estimate[, , 1]
  cat("max | |P_varm| - |P_vars| | =", sci(max(abs(abs(unname(P)) - abs(unname(bq$B))))), "(columns match up to sign)\n")
}
#> max | |P_varm| - |P_vars| | = 1.7e-13 (columns match up to sign)

2.3 Local projections against lm + sandwich

For each response and horizon, LP is an OLS regression of yt+hy_{t+h} on the shock and controls. The comparison builds the same regression by hand with lm() and takes the Newey-West (Bartlett, lag h+1h+1, no prewhitening, no small-sample factor) and HC1 variances from sandwich.

if (have("sandwich")) {
  n <- nrow(Y); p <- 3; H <- 6
  lead <- function(x, h) if (h == 0) x else c(x[-(1:h)], rep(NA, h))
  lagm <- function(x, l) c(rep(NA, l), x[1:(n - l)])
  dfL <- data.frame(Y)
  for (l in 1:p) for (v in colnames(Y)) dfL[[paste0(v, ".l", l)]] <- lagm(Y[, v], l)
  ctr <- paste(c("infl", "unemp", setdiff(names(dfL), colnames(Y))), collapse = "+")
  manual <- function(h, v) {
    d <- dfL; d$yy <- lead(Y[, v], h); d <- d[(p + 1):(n - h), ]
    lm(as.formula(paste("yy ~ rate +", ctr)), d)
  }
  f_nw <- lp(Y, shock = "rate", horizon = H, lags = p, contemp = c("infl", "unemp"))
  f_hc <- lp(Y, shock = "rate", horizon = H, lags = p, contemp = c("infl", "unemp"), se = "hc")
  d_b <- d_nw <- d_hc <- 0
  suppressWarnings(for (h in 0:H) for (v in colnames(Y)) {
    fm <- manual(h, v)
    d_b <- max(d_b, abs(f_nw$estimate[h + 1, v] - coef(fm)[["rate"]]))
    d_nw <- max(d_nw, abs(f_nw$se[h + 1, v] -
      sqrt(sandwich::NeweyWest(fm, lag = h + 1, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = FALSE)["rate", "rate"])))
    d_hc <- max(d_hc, abs(f_hc$se[h + 1, v] - sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(fm, "HC1")["rate", "rate"])))
  })
  tibble::tibble(quantity = c("LP coefficient", "Newey-West se", "HC1 se"),
                 max_abs_diff = sci(c(d_b, d_nw, d_hc)), horizons = "0..6, all 3 responses")
}
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   quantity       max_abs_diff horizons             
#>   <chr>          <chr>        <chr>                
#> 1 LP coefficient 7.3e-14      0..6, all 3 responses
#> 2 Newey-West se  2.7e-13      0..6, all 3 responses
#> 3 HC1 se         2.9e-13      0..6, all 3 responses

2.4 State-dependent LP against lpirfs::lp_nl

lp_state(timing = "lagged") reproduces the lpirfs convention (logistic state weight on the lagged HP-filtered indicator, interacted lag-1 coefficients, Cholesky columns of the linear VAR). One configuration is run live; the second configuration (levels-standardised state, trend, a different shock type) is in validation/lp-extra.R, and its output is quoted in section 3.4.

if (have("lpirfs")) {
  H <- 8; df <- as.data.frame(yraw)
  ref <- suppressMessages(lpirfs::lp_nl(df, lags_endog_lin = 2, lags_endog_nl = 2, trend = 0, shock_type = 0,
                       confint = 1, hor = H, switching = yraw$infl, use_hp = 1, lambda = 1600,
                       gamma = 3, use_nw = TRUE, num_cores = 1))
  d <- sapply(1:3, function(sj) {
    me <- lp_state(yraw, all_of(sj), "infl", H, lags = 2, timing = "lagged", lags_lin = 2, shock_type = 0,
                   gamma = 3, hp_lambda = 1600, state_const = FALSE, trend = FALSE)
    c(high = max(abs(me$estimate[, , "high"] - t(ref$irf_s1_mean[, , sj]))),
      low = max(abs(me$estimate[, , "low"] - t(ref$irf_s2_mean[, , sj]))))
  })
  colnames(d) <- paste("shock", 1:3)
  apply(d, 1:2, sci)
}
#>      shock 1   shock 2   shock 3  
#> high "1.5e-13" "2.4e-13" "2.6e-13"
#> low  "2.2e-13" "3.1e-13" "4.0e-13"

2.5 Hierarchical Bayesian VAR: log posterior against BVAR

BVAR::bvar() optimises the log posterior of the hyperparameters (λ,μ,θ,ψ)(\lambda, \mu, \theta, \psi) (overall tightness, sum-of-coefficients, single-unit-root, prior scale). Evaluating the varm log posterior at the same point (with the same psi and the same hyperprior parameters) must give the same value. The comparison is deterministic, so any difference is numerical rounding. It uses internal helper functions (varm:::cpp_niw_logpost).

if (have("BVAR")) {
  p <- 4
  set.seed(1)
  bv <- suppressWarnings(BVAR::bvar(Y, lags = p, n_draw = 400, n_burn = 100, n_thin = 1,
        priors = BVAR::bv_priors(hyper = "auto", mn = BVAR::bv_mn(), soc = BVAR::bv_soc(), sur = BVAR::bv_sur()),
        verbose = FALSE))
  ols <- varm:::cpp_var_ols(Y, p, matrix(1, nrow(Y), 1))
  b <- matrix(0, 13, 3); b[cbind(1:3, 1:3)] <- 1
  gamma_coef <- varm:::gamma_coef
  gp <- rbind(gamma_coef(.2, .4), gamma_coef(2, .25), gamma_coef(1, 1), gamma_coef(1, 1))
  h <- c(bv$optim$par[["lambda"]], 2, bv$optim$par[["soc"]], bv$optim$par[["sur"]], bv$priors$psi$mode)
  # BVAR takes its dummy means from the regression sample, so pass those rows here (bvarm() uses the presample)
  v <- varm:::cpp_niw_logpost(h, ols$Y, ols$X, p, 1L, TRUE, b, 1e7, colMeans(ols$Y[1:p, ]), 1, c(1L, 0L, 1L, 1L, 0L, 0L, 0L), gp,
                              c(1e-4, 1, 1e-4, 1e-4, 0, 0, 0), c(5, 3, 50, 50, Inf, Inf, Inf), c(.004, .004), FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("log posterior: BVAR %.10f  varm %.10f  |diff| = %s (relative %s)\n",
              bv$optim$value, v, sci(abs(v - bv$optim$value)), sci(abs(v - bv$optim$value) / abs(v))))
}
#> log posterior: BVAR -403.7381334206  varm -403.7381334206  |diff| = 1.0e-12 (relative 2.5e-15)

2.6 Draw-based IRFs: consistency of the three uncertainty engines

There is no external reference for the bands, so this check is internal: the bootstrap, the asymptotic Monte Carlo and the Bayesian sampler should produce bands of similar width for the same data when the Bayesian prior is loose. This is a consistency check, not a proof of correctness.

set.seed(11)
f <- varm(Y, p = 2)
b_boot <- irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 1000)
b_mc   <- irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "mc", nboot = 1000)
bf <- bvarm(Y, p = 2, prior_minnesota(lambda = c(5, 1, 1e-4, 50), soc = NULL, sur = NULL, hyper = character(0)),
            ndraw = 1000)
b_bay <- irf(bf, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12)

# one tidy() frame per engine: response of unemp to a rate shock, 90% band
cell <- function(ir, engine) {
  d <- tidy(ir)
  d <- d[d$response == "unemp" & d$shock == "rate" & d$level == 0.9, ]
  d$engine <- engine
  d
}
d <- rbind(cell(b_boot, "bootstrap"), cell(b_mc, "asymptotic MC"), cell(b_bay, "loose BVAR"))
aggregate(cbind(width = conf.high - conf.low) ~ engine, data = d, FUN = mean) |>
  transform(width = round(width, 3))
#>          engine width
#> 1 asymptotic MC 0.111
#> 2     bootstrap 0.112
#> 3    loose BVAR 0.106
ggplot(d, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = engine, fill = engine)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(3)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(3)) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (quarters)", y = "Response of unemp to rate", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_varm()

(Mean width of the 90% band of the response of unemp to rate, horizons 0 to 12, and the bands themselves.)

2.7 The tidy layer is a lossless view of the objects

tidy(), glance() and autoplot() are thin layers over the stored arrays; the unit tests cover them. Live, the tibbles reproduce the internals exactly and every plot builds:

f <- varm(Y, p = 2)
ir <- irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "none")
td <- tidy(ir)
lpf <- lp(Y, shock = rate, contemp = c(infl, unemp), horizon = 6, lags = 2)
tl <- tidy(lpf, conf.int = FALSE)
tibble::tibble(
  check = c("tidy(varm) vs coef()", "tidy(irf) vs $estimate", "tidy(lp) vs $estimate"),
  max_abs_diff = sci(c(
    max(abs(tidy(f)$estimate - as.vector(coef(f)))),
    max(abs(td$estimate - ir$estimate[cbind(as.integer(td$response), as.integer(td$shock), td$horizon + 1)])),
    max(abs(tl$estimate - lpf$estimate[cbind(tl$horizon + 1, as.integer(tl$response))]))
  ))
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   check                  max_abs_diff
#>   <chr>                  <chr>       
#> 1 tidy(varm) vs coef()   0.0e+00     
#> 2 tidy(irf) vs $estimate 0.0e+00     
#> 3 tidy(lp) vs $estimate  0.0e+00
glance(f)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>       K     p  nobs logLik   AIC   BIC    HQ max_root
#>   <int> <int> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     3     2   213  -338.  731.  822.  768.    0.946
inherits(autoplot(ir), "ggplot") && inherits(autoplot(lpf), "ggplot")
#> [1] TRUE

3. Quoted results of the longer scripts

Each block shows the output of the stated command. They are not recomputed when the vignette is built.

3.1 Bayesian engines: Rscript validation/bayes.R

Triangular sampler against an exact posterior (s1). With homoskedastic errors the triangular prior is semi-conjugate, so the posterior of each equation has a one-dimensional-quadrature form. The sampler’s draws are compared with it by zz-scores of posterior means and variance ratios.

[PASS] 1a K=1 matches exact semi-conjugate posterior  max|z|= 2.22  var ratio range 0.997-1.018
[PASS] 1b K=3 reduced-form (B, Sigma, A) vs exact structural posterior  max|z| B/Sigma/A: 1.61 1.52 1.59
[PASS] 1c loose prior reproduces OLS  max|B-OLS|= 0.00121  (Sigma mean rel dev  0.066 )

Stochastic volatility (s2). The Kim-Shephard-Chib mixture is an approximation of the log⁡χ12\log\chi^2_1 density, so the Geweke joint-distribution test is run with tolerance |z|<4|z|<4 rather than 2.

Geweke z (sig2,h0,hT,mean h): 0.61 -1.05 -0.94 -0.99  var ratios: 1.002 0.998 0.999 0.998
[PASS] 2a Geweke joint-distribution test (KSC approx; mixture is approximate, tolerance |z|<4)
eq1 (tv): cor(h)=0.965 90% coverage=0.82 ; sigma_h posterior mean=0.084 (true 0.12)
eq2 (const): 90% coverage=0.98 ; mean sd of h2 path=0.234; sigma_h mean=0.074 (true 0, prior mean 0.1)
[PASS] 2b time-varying vol recovery
[PASS] 2b constant vol recovered (sigma_h shrinks, coverage)
[PASS] 2c Sigma = A^-1 Lambda A^-T algebra (last-period vol)  max err 0

Note the 90% credible band of the true volatility path covers 82% in the time-varying equation, and the posterior mean of the volatility-of-volatility σh\sigma_h is 0.084 against a truth of 0.12 (one dataset).

Simulation-based calibration of σh2\sigma_h^2 (s2d). Truths are drawn from the prior, data are simulated, and the 90% credible interval of σh2\sigma_h^2 and of the log-volatility path are checked (60 replications):

rank histogram (quintiles) of true sigma_h^2 in posterior: 6 9 14 13 18
[PASS] 2d sigma_h^2 90% credible-interval coverage (prior-drawn truths)  cov= 0.833  mean vol-path 90% coverage= 0.883

The coverage of σh2\sigma_h^2 is 0.83 against a nominal 0.90, and the rank histogram is tilted toward high ranks (true value ranked high in the posterior, i.e. the posterior of σh2\sigma_h^2 is a little too low). With 60 replications the standard error of a coverage estimate is about 0.04, so the shortfall is suggestive rather than conclusive; see section 5.

Shrinkage priors (s3).

[PASS] 3a SSVS inclusion separates true nonzeros from zeros  P(incl|nonzero)= 0.903  P(incl|zero)= 0.199
[PASS] 3b horseshoe/SSVS beat OLS RMSE; horseshoe shrinks zeros  rmse hs/ssvs/ols= 0.0362 0.0351 0.0717

Conjugate NIW sampler (s4). Fixed hyperparameters: draws against the analytic NIW moments. Hierarchical: posterior means of the hyperparameters against an exact quadrature, and against BVAR’s own MCMC.

[PASS] 4a fixed-hyper draws vs analytic ...  z= 3.26  Sigma rel= 0.0013  var rel= 0.0155  corr maxdiff= 0.0134
      lambda    soc    sur
varm  0.9747 0.3682 0.6843
BVAR  0.9869 0.3652 0.6107
exact 0.9800 0.3749 0.6651
[PASS] 4b hierarchical hyper means: varm MCMC vs exact quadrature (within 5%)  rel diffs 0.005 0.018 0.029 | BVAR's own MCMC vs exact: 0.007 0.026 0.082
[PASS] 4c posterior mean of B vs BVAR   max |posterior mean B diff| = 0.00516

The max zz of 3.26 (over all coefficients; the script’s threshold is 4.5) is the weakest of the agreement numbers in this block. The draws are iid here, so this is a single large-ish order statistic rather than evidence of autocorrelation, but it is the number to look at if the fixed-hyperparameter sampler is ever changed.

3.2 Coverage of draw-based IRF bands (s6)

Design: Cholesky IRFs of a bivariate VAR(1), T=200T=200, 300 replications, 400 draws each, averaged over the 2×2×132\times2\times13 responses; “bc” is Kilian bias correction. The persistence is ρ=0.9\rho=0.9.

IRF coverage, iid errors
  method cov68 cov90   w68   w90
     iid 0.593 0.809 0.128 0.211
  iid_bc 0.674 0.893 0.156 0.256
    wild 0.552 0.754 0.120 0.196
 wild_bc 0.622 0.831 0.146 0.239
      mc 0.653 0.876 0.136 0.231

IRF coverage, heteroskedastic errors
  method cov68 cov90   w68   w90
     iid 0.475 0.701 0.210 0.345
  iid_bc 0.385 0.610 0.254 0.419
    wild 0.531 0.753 0.223 0.365
 wild_bc 0.437 0.655 0.283 0.461
      mc 0.420 0.614 0.218 0.370

What these numbers say:

  • With persistent data (ρ=0.9\rho=0.9) and T=200T=200, only the bias-corrected iid bootstrap (0.893) and the Monte Carlo (0.876) are close to the nominal 90%. The plain iid bootstrap covers 81%, the plain wild bootstrap 75%.
  • Under heteroskedasticity every method under-covers; the wild bootstrap (0.753) is the best of them but still 15 points below nominal. The bias-corrected versions are worse there (0.61-0.66).
  • The script’s pass criteria are relative (“within 0.07 of nominal” for the iid design with the chosen methods; “wild at least as good as iid” for the heteroskedastic one), which is weaker than “nominal coverage achieved”.

Coverage of the two newer Bayesian proxy-SVAR samplers (varm_proxy_arw(), varm_proxy_gkr()), K=3K=3 VAR(1), T=300T=300, 50 replications (Rscript validation/proxy-bayes-full.R; with 50 replications a coverage estimate has a standard error of about 0.04 to 0.07):

 arw68  arw90  gkr_set  gkr_rcr  gkr_bayes90  w_rcr  w_bayes
 0.690  0.910  0.573    0.907    0.647        0.852  0.708

arw68/arw90 are the coverages of the 68% and 90% posterior bands for the impact responses to the proxied shock. For the set-identified shock, gkr_set is how often the truth lies inside the estimated set of posterior means (0.57, so the set of posterior means alone is not a confidence set), gkr_rcr is the coverage of the 90% robust credible region (0.91) and gkr_bayes90 that of the conventional single-prior 90% band (0.65); w_rcr and w_bayes are the mean widths (0.85 against 0.71).

4. Timing

All numbers are seconds of elapsed time on an Apple M4 Pro (R 4.6.1, OpenBLAS, single-threaded with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, nothing else running), with the installed package. Reproduce the Bayesian block with Rscript validation/bayes.R s8 (its DGP: T=250T=250, p=4p=4, 1000 retained draws; the numbers below come from the installed package, s8 through pkgload::load_all() gave the same values to within about 0.2 s except the hierarchical K=3K=3 row, 0.12 s against 0.08 s).

seconds per 1000 draws K = 3 K = 7 K = 20
bvarm, conjugate, fixed hyperparameters 0.003 0.010 0.061
bvarm, conjugate, hierarchical (optimiser + MH, 500 burn-in) 0.054 0.177 1.271
bvarm, triangular Minnesota, homoskedastic (200 burn-in) 0.019 0.110 1.312
bvarm, triangular horseshoe, homoskedastic 0.05 0.28 5.92
bvarm, triangular Minnesota + stochastic volatility 0.112 0.382 2.979
BVAR::bvar (hierarchical λ\lambda) 0.157 0.259 0.899
bsvars::bsvar_sv (structural SV, S=1000S=1000) 1.35 4.64 not run

Honest reading, comparing the hierarchical conjugate sampler with BVAR::bvar (the closest like-for-like): varm is about three times as fast at K=3K=3 (0.054 against 0.157 s), faster at K=7K=7 (0.177 against 0.259 s) and slower at K=20K=20 (1.27 against 0.90 s). The two samplers are not identical (varm also runs an optimiser before the Metropolis chain; the triangular and SV samplers have no BVAR counterpart, and BVAR::bvar is at 0.157 s for K=3K=3 against 0.112 s for varm with SV, which is a different model). The K=20K=20 timing was identical with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, so it is not a threading artefact. Other models on yraw (T=215T=215, K=3K=3, p=2p=2):

  • tvpvar() with SV, time-varying AtA_t and full QQ, 10000 draws and 2000 burn-in sweeps (T=215T=215, K=3K=3, p=2p=2; estimation sample 173): about 8 s on an otherwise idle machine. Timings taken while other jobs were running were up to four times higher, so quote them only from a quiet machine. Cost grows with pp.
  • A full 3-variable lp() (17 horizons, 3 responses): about 0.5 ms per call; varm() OLS about 0.05 ms. One thousand wild-bootstrap draws of a VAR(2): 0.02 s; the IRF with wild bands (1000 draws, 17 horizons): 0.03 s. (Best of three runs on an Apple M4 Pro with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1.)

5. Failures and limitations found

These are the findings of the checks above that a user should know about.

  1. Proxy-SVAR wild bootstrap does not cover the normalised impact response. In validation/proxy-coverage.R, the wild-bootstrap 90% interval for the impact response (h=0h=0) covers 13.5% (strong instrument) and 21% (weak instrument) of the time, and 0.15 in ident-extra.R. The interval is very narrow (median width 0.027 against 0.20 for the block bootstrap); the cause was not investigated here. Use type = "mbb" (moving block bootstrap, Jentsch and Lunsford) or varm_proxy_robust(). At horizons 1 to 8 the wild bootstrap covers 81-85% (strong instrument), still below nominal. The moving-block bootstrap covers 77-87% with a strong instrument, i.e. under-covers somewhat at this TT.
  2. Weak-instrument robust sets are infinite, as they should be. With median F=2F=2 the MOSW sets have infinite width and cover 88-94%; the bootstrap intervals have finite width but the moving-block one is very wide at h=0h=0 (3.76) and its coverage is 0.86-0.945.
  3. Stochastic-volatility calibration is slightly under-covering. The volatility-of-volatility interval covers 83% (nominal 90%, 60 replications) and the time-varying-equation path covers 82%; the posterior of σh\sigma_h tends to be low (0.084 against 0.12). The Kim-Shephard-Chib mixture is itself an approximation (Geweke test needs tolerance |z|<4|z|<4).
  4. Bootstrap coverage under persistence and heteroskedasticity. With ρ=0.9\rho=0.9, T=200T=200 the plain bootstrap covers 75-81% at the 90% level, and under heteroskedastic errors every draw-based method covers 61-75%; Kilian’s bias correction helps with iid errors and hurts with heteroskedastic errors (section 3.2). Treat 90% bands from a short, persistent, heteroskedastic sample as approximately 70-75% bands.
  5. Sup-t bands under-cover in the simulation. Whole-path coverage is 0.78 with HAC errors and 0.84 with lag-augmented HC errors, against a nominal 0.90, but the pointwise band covers the whole path only 24% of the time, so the sup-t adjustment is a large improvement though not complete. The shortfall is the finite-sample undercoverage of HAC/HC errors carried over.
  6. Hierarchical NIW sampler mixes slowly. mcmc_diagnostics() on a bvarm fit of yraw with 3000 retained draws and 1000 burn-in (one chain) reported effective sample sizes of about 158 (λ\lambda), 72 (soc) and 89 (sur) (split R-hat 1.00-1.01), against 3000 draws. Run several chains or increase ndraw when you need tail probabilities of the hyperparameters. The posterior means agree with the exact quadrature to 0.5-3% (section 3.1).
  7. TVP-VAR path coverage depends on the prior. When the data are generated from the sampler’s own prior, 90% bands cover 0.91/0.94/0.89 (beta, AA, log-volatility). When the data come from a simulated TVP-SV process (T=250T=250, K=3K=3) and the sampler uses the data-driven training-sample prior, coverage depends on the prior tightness kQk_Q: with the default kQ=0.01k_Q=0.01 the coefficient bands cover 56% and the log-variance bands 65% (8 replications, so large uncertainty); with kQ=0.05k_Q=0.05 it is 79% and 68%. Choose tvp_prior(kQ = ) with care and check the sensitivity.
  8. Speed claims are specific to the machine and the settings (section 4). BVAR::bvar is faster at K=20K=20.
  9. Differences from the MATLAB toolboxes are conventions, not errors. The BEAR, VAR-Toolbox and BVAR_ comparisons (validation/DIARY.md) found these differences: the Minnesota AR variance divisor is n−pn-p here and n−2p−1n-2p-1 in BEAR; alpha is twice BEAR’s lambda3; the inverse-Wishart degrees of freedom are T−kT-k here and T−k−K−1T-k-K-1 in BVAR_; bootstrap residuals are rescaled by Te/(Te−m)\sqrt{T_e/(T_e-m)} (bands 6-7% wider than VAR-Toolbox, undocumented in ?draws); forecast bands include parameter uncertainty (BEAR’s do not); fevd() under id_proxy returns 100% for the proxy shock (VAR-Toolbox: 17% at h=48h=48 on Gertler-Karadi data).
  10. Zero-filled proxies are only neutral for a mean-zero instrument. The proxy functions zero-fill missing instrument values and use uncentred moments. This leaves normalised responses unchanged only if the instrument has mean zero on its observed sample; on the Gertler-Karadi data the IRFs move by 1.6-4.6%. Demean the instrument on its observed sample first.
  11. Dummy-observation priors were corrected after the toolbox comparison. The sum-of-coefficients and single-unit-root dummies now use the pp presample observations (they used observations p+1p+1 to 2p2p), the unit-root dummy covers exogenous columns, and the marginal likelihood updates the dummy block’s posterior (it gave -595.5 against -630.4 for BEAR’s formula on one example). After the fix the BEAR posterior checks agree within Monte Carlo error. The log marginal likelihood with sum-of-coefficients alone equals BEAR’s formula; with both dummies together it still differs by 0.045 log units, not yet explained.

6. What has not been validated

  • The Bayesian proxy-SVAR variants (varm_proxy_bayes(), varm_proxy_arw(), varm_proxy_gkr()) are checked for internal consistency, against the bootstrap with a strong proxy (varm_proxy_bayes()) and by the coverage simulation in section 3.3; there is no comparison with a published replication.
  • lp_panel() is checked against lm with dummy variables and hand-coded cluster errors on an unbalanced panel, not against plm or fixest.
  • id_hetero() recovers the impact matrix in a two-regime simulation; there is no external reference implementation compared.
  • forecast() is checked for the point forecast against vars; density forecasts and hd() are not compared with another package.
  • The MATLAB toolboxes were not run. The BEAR, VAR-Toolbox and BVAR_ checks use R ports of their .m code (BEAR’s ports are also checked against its stored .mat results; the other two only by internal consistency). Methods with no varm counterpart (narrative signs, FAVAR, mixed-frequency, panel and threshold VARs, conditional forecasts) and BEAR’s stochastic-volatility and TVP models are not compared.
  • The comparisons against vars, BVAR, lpirfs, bsvars and svars need those packages to load; on the machine used for the last run they did not (stale library paths under Homebrew R), so those tests were skipped.
  • Missing values are rejected with an error (not handled), and nothing here covers VARs larger than K=20K=20.
